lesson.title: The Address of a Point: Ordered Pairs
lesson.summary: An ordered pair (x, y) locates a single point on the coordinate plane, and the order of its two coordinates always matters.
lesson.body:
An ordered pair is a pair of numbers written in the form (x, y) that gives the exact address of a single point on the coordinate plane you met in the last chapter. The first number, the x-coordinate, tells you how far to move horizontally from the origin, right if positive and left if negative. The second number, the y-coordinate, tells you how far to move vertically from that spot, up if positive and down if negative. Together those two instructions locate exactly one point, and no other pair of instructions locates that same point.

The word ordered is not decoration, it is the whole point of the notation: the order in which the two numbers are written changes which point they describe. The ordered pair (3, 5) means move 3 units right and 5 units up, landing in Quadrant I. The ordered pair (5, 3) means move 5 units right and 3 units up instead, a completely different location, also in Quadrant I but not the same point at all. Swapping the coordinates of an ordered pair almost always produces a different point, the only exception being when the two coordinates happen to be equal, like (4, 4).

Ordered pairs are also the natural language for describing a function's graph. Every point plotted on the graph of a function f is an ordered pair of the form (x, f(x)), the input paired with the one output that function assigns to it. This is exactly why the vertical line test works the way it does: two ordered pairs with the same x-coordinate but different y-coordinates, like (3, 4) and (3, -4) from the circle example earlier in this unit, cannot both belong to a function, because that would mean the input 3 produces two different outputs.

Consider the function f(x) = 2x - 1, and generate the ordered pairs it produces at three inputs. At x = -1: f(-1) = 2(-1) - 1 = -2 - 1 = -3, giving the ordered pair (-1, -3). At x = 0: f(0) = 2(0) - 1 = 0 - 1 = -1, giving the ordered pair (0, -1). At x = 2: f(2) = 2(2) - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3, giving the ordered pair (2, 3). Plotting (-1, -3), (0, -1), and (2, 3) on the coordinate plane and connecting them reveals a straight, unbroken line, confirming that this particular function is continuous rather than discrete, since every real x between these three points would generate a valid ordered pair as well.

Ordered pairs are not limited to describing function outputs; they are also how you record and check solutions to any equation in two variables. To verify that (2, 3) is a solution to 3x - y = 3, substitute directly: 3(2) - 3 = 6 - 3 = 3, which matches the right-hand side, so the ordered pair checks out and the point belongs on that equation's graph. This same substitute-and-check process works no matter whether the two-variable relationship you are checking turns out to be a function, a circle, or any other curve on the coordinate plane.

From the vertical line test all the way through translations and reflections, every idea in this unit has really been a statement about ordered pairs: which ones are allowed to share an x-coordinate, which ones are isolated dots versus connected curves, and which ones slide or flip to new locations under a transformation. The ordered pair is the smallest building block underneath all of it, the single ounce of information, an input matched with an output, that every graph in algebra is made from.
